_about: The astronomy problem book's registry: key books and named classics. See principles/problem-books.md. Every named classic here is solved in a problem set; "where" points to it.
intro: Astronomy problems turn a few laws of physics into facts about objects no one will ever visit. Each set asks for a guess first, then the calculation, then a comparison with what telescopes see.
lede: Climb the ladder from Level 1, or pick a scale from the Solar System to the whole universe, and guess before you calculate.

stage.title: From planets to the universe
stage.blurb: Three sets that move outwards in scale, each running from warm-ups to hard problems, every one with a worked solution.

books.title: An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics
books.author: Bradley W. Carroll & Dale A. Ostlie
books.when: The standard undergraduate text, with hundreds of problems. Alongside any of the three sets.

books.title: Fundamental Astronomy
books.author: Hannu Karttunen and others
books.when: Spherical astronomy, orbits and stellar physics with worked examples. After P1.

books.title: Problem Book in Relativity and Gravitation
books.author: Alan P. Lightman, William H. Press, Richard H. Price & Saul A. Teukolsky
books.when: Five hundred problems with full solutions on relativity, black holes and cosmology. After P3, for the boss problems.

books.title: Introduction to Cosmology
books.author: Barbara Ryden
books.when: Friedmann's equation to inflation, with clear exercises. After P3 problems 6–11.

books.title: Astrophysics in a Nutshell
books.author: Dan Maoz
books.when: Short, physical and full of order-of-magnitude reasoning. After P2.

books.title: Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students
books.author: Howard D. Curtis
books.when: Turns P1's transfers and slingshots into real mission design.

books.title: Astronomy (OpenStax)
books.author: Andrew Fraknoi, David Morrison & Sidney C. Wolff
books.when: A free survey of the whole subject, good background reading before any set.

hard.title: Orbits are conic sections
hard.idea: The Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector is conserved under an inverse-square force; one dot product turns it into the equation of a conic.
hard.visual: An orbit with its fixed Runge–Lenz arrow pointing at perihelion.

hard.title: Launch sideways from 1 AU
hard.idea: Vis-viva: the orbit's size depends only on the energy. Below √2 times circular speed the orbit closes; above it, it escapes.
hard.visual: Circle, ellipse, parabola and hyperbola from one slider (interactive).

hard.title: A trip to Mars
hard.idea: Two burns of about 3 km/s, 259 days, and Mars must lead the Earth by 44° at launch.
hard.visual: The transfer ellipse touching both orbits, with the planets at launch and arrival.

hard.title: The Hill sphere
hard.idea: A planet controls space out to a(m/3M)^(1/3): 1.5 million km for the Earth, where L1 and L2 sit.
hard.visual: The effective potential in the rotating frame, with the saddle at L1.

hard.title: The lengthening day
hard.idea: The Moon recedes 3.8 cm a year; conserving angular momentum lengthens the day by about 2 ms per century.
hard.visual: Day length and Moon distance traced back through geological time.

hard.title: A lower bound on the Sun's central pressure
hard.idea: P + GM(r)²/8πr⁴ decreases outwards, so any star's centre is crushed by at least GM²/8πR⁴.
hard.visual: Pressure against radius for different density profiles, all above the bound.

hard.title: Fusion by tunnelling
hard.idea: The Boltzmann tail falls and the tunnelling probability rises with energy; their product peaks at 6 keV, about 4.5 kT.
hard.visual: The two factors and their narrow product, the Gamow peak.

hard.title: The heaviest star
hard.idea: Radiation pressure on electrons balances gravity on protons at L = 4πGMm_p c/σ_T, capping stars at roughly a hundred Suns.
hard.visual: L against M on a log plot: the mass–luminosity law meeting the Eddington line.

hard.title: Chandrasekhar's limit
hard.idea: For relativistic electrons, degeneracy pressure and gravity scale the same way with radius, leaving one mass: 1.44 Suns.
hard.visual: White-dwarf radius against mass, falling to zero at the limit.

hard.title: Why is the night sky dark?
hard.idea: In an infinite eternal universe every shell is equally bright. A finite age wins by a factor of a hundred trillion.
hard.visual: Shells of stars, each contributing the same light.

hard.title: A universe younger than its stars
hard.idea: Matter alone gives an age of 2/3H₀ = 9.3 billion years, younger than the oldest stars; dark energy fixes it at 13.5.
hard.visual: Scale factor against time for matter-only and ΛCDM universes.

hard.title: The horizon problem
hard.idea: Patches of the CMB more than about 2° apart were never in contact, yet share a temperature to 1 part in 100,000.
hard.visual: A conformal diagram with the light cones of two CMB points not overlapping.

hard.title: GPS needs relativity
hard.idea: Orbiting clocks run 45.7 μs a day fast from gravity and 7.2 slow from speed: without the correction, 11 km of error a day.
hard.visual: The two effects against orbital radius, crossing at 1.5 Earth radii.
